analysis.one_liner: Ends every federal tax under the tax code after 2001, with no replacement specified.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have shut off every tax collected under the federal tax code — income tax, payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare, estate and gift taxes, and excise taxes — after December 31, 2001. It does not create a replacement tax system; it only states that Congress 'declares' any new system should be simple and fair, with a low rate for everyone and a supermajority needed to raise taxes. In practice, terminating the tax code without naming a replacement would have ended federal tax collection and left funding for the entire government, including Social Security and Medicare, to whatever Congress passed later.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the biggest winners would be the highest earners and the largest estates, because the income tax is progressive and the estate and gift taxes fall only on large inheritances. Every taxpayer would owe less in the short run, but Social Security and Medicare are funded by payroll taxes collected under the same code, so their financing would lapse unless a new system was enacted first.

how_it_helps.text: Terminates all taxes imposed by the Internal Revenue Code for any year beginning after December 31, 2001, including income, payroll, estate, gift, and excise taxes [S3].

Declares that any replacement system should apply a low rate to all Americans, provide tax relief for working Americans, eliminate the bias against savings and investment, and protect Social Security and Medicare [S3].
Would require a supermajority of both houses of Congress to raise taxes under any new system [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries and everyone who depends on federal programs, since the payroll taxes and income taxes that fund them would stop with no replacement named. Whoever bore the burden of whatever new tax Congress eventually passed — which the bill does not specify — would pay after 2001.

drawbacks.text: The bill ends payroll tax collection that funds Social Security and Medicare without enacting a replacement, only 'declaring' that a new system should protect them — leaving the government's largest programs with no guaranteed funding [S3].

Because the income tax is progressive, abolishing it with no named replacement would cut taxes most, in dollar terms, for high earners while leaving unclear who would pay for the government afterward [S3].
A tax code that simply expires on a date certain, with no successor enacted, would create immediate funding uncertainty for federal operations and markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The short-term tax relief would be broad, but the bill is essentially a statement of principles rather than a workable law: it kills every federal tax on a fixed date without legislating a successor. The serious cost is that Social Security, Medicare, and all federal spending would lose their funding source unless Congress enacted an entirely new system first, and the bill only expresses hopes about what that system would look like.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Hutchinson introduced the bill on September 26, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action — no markup, no hearing, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1999, so the bill expired without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died, the federal government's tax collection — including the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare — continued uninterrupted, and the public avoided the risk of losing program funding with no replacement in place. Anyone counting on Social Security or Medicare benefits was better protected by the bill's failure.

for.name: Sen. Tim Hutchinson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to terminate the tax code after 2001.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up after referral; no markup, hearing, or vote was scheduled.

against.name: William Roth
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Republican-run Finance Committee gave it no action.

industries.note: Repealing the progressive income tax and the estate and gift taxes would deliver the largest tax cuts, in dollar terms, to the highest earners and the biggest inheritances, while the bill leaves unspecified who would fund the government instead.

The corporate income tax and taxes on investment gains are imposed by the same code and would end after 2001, and the bill calls for a new system that eliminates the bias against savings and investment.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Terminating the code without a successor would wipe out the compliance burden that drives demand for tax preparation services — but any new system Congress wrote could create its own, possibly larger, compliance industry.
